articles.title: These AI agents design your perfect robot-powered lab — and run it for you
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03587-xA team of artificial-intelligence agents simulates a laboratory of robots and instruments to ensure that the physical workspace functions smoothly and then directs that workspace’s operations.
articles.content:
Artificial-intelligence agents can devise a detailed procedure for a robotic arm and test it in a virtual laboratory.Credit: Jiaru Bai & Yuchi Zhao, University of Toronto

Laboratory robots are tireless and uncomplaining, but they have narrow skill sets, limited mobility and an inability to get out of each other’s way. Now, a system of artificial-intelligence agents promises to help lab robots do their best work.

In this process, a scientist describes their research programme and lab set-up to the agents, which then create step-by-step experimental protocols for the lab’s robots. The agents also generate a virtual version of the lab and test the protocols there. They can then direct the robots in the real lab to perform the research.

Robot chemist sparks row with claim it created new materials

The agents can even design an entire lab from scratch, using a virtual one to work out the ideal placement for instruments and robots.

The system is described in a preprint posted in October to arXiv1. It has not been peer reviewed.

In a test, the agents wrote more than 200 commands directing a robotic arm to move between and interact with instruments in an existing lab space. The agent simulated the steps in the virtual lab to ensure that it all worked smoothly, then directed the real-life arm to carry out procedures to measure the optical properties of nanocrystals.

The concept is “very cool” and could drastically reduce the effort required to set up automated labs, says Evan Collins, a bioengineer at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge. But integrating the cameras and sensors that the agents need to direct experiments effectively could require more resources than does setting up a lab manually, he says.

Collision avoidance

The simulations would make it easy to plan robotic movements that avoid collisions between robots and other objects in the lab, says Collins.

This could ease the process of getting labs up and running, given that setting up an automated lab is often a time-consuming process of trial and error followed by extensive testing and troubleshooting. Because the agents conduct all the planning and testing in a simulated environment, there is no need for researchers to “babysit the system” after it’s built, says Yuchi (Allan) Zhao, a roboticist at the University of Toronto in Canada and co-author of the preprint.
articles.reasoning: The article describes an AI system that designs and manages robotic labs by simulating and optimizing workflows virtually before real-world implementation. This innovation promises to significantly reduce the time, effort, and errors involved in setting up automated labs, potentially accelerating scientific research and experimentation on a broad scale. The story focuses on a single technological breakthrough with clear, tangible benefits for the scientific community and beyond.

articles.title: Record-breaking, fast-spinning magnet could help uncover new physics
articles.summary: A magnet barely wider than a human hair is one of the fastest spinning objects ever and could be useful for both fundamental physics experiments and in quantum technology
articles.content:
A magnet barely wider than a human hair is one of the fastest spinning objects ever and could be useful for both fundamental physics experiments and in quantum technology

Magnets can be made to levitate by the Meissner effect Science History Images / Alamy

A tiny magnet that levitates within a superconductor trap may be the fastest spinning object visible to the naked eye, and one of the fastest spinning objects ever made. In the future, it could be used in experiments searching for mysterious dark matter particles and aid the development of quantum technologies.

Superconductors are materials that conduct electricity with perfect efficiency, and they also expel any magnetic field that tries to permeate them – a phenomenon known as the Meissner effect. Because of this, a magnet placed above a superconductor experiences repulsive magnetic forces and starts to levitate. Tao Wang at the Agency for Science Technology and Research in Singapore and his colleagues have now set one such levitating magnet spinning at an unprecedently fast rate.

The researchers used a spherical magnet made from neodymium, iron and boron that was about 30 micrometres wide, similar to the width of a fine human hair. They placed it in a cylindrical container made from lead, then enclosed that container in a chamber devoid of air, or a vacuum chamber.

Advertisement

Next, they used liquid helium to cool the whole setup to approximately -269°C (-452°F), only a few degrees above the coldest possible temperature. Under these extreme circumstances, lead behaved as a superconductor and the lack of air meant that the magnet could levitate within it without bumping into any particles. The team set the magnet spinning with a magnetic coil, ultimately pushing this tiny rotor to 138 million revolutions per minute.

Wang says the magnet’s spinning was also very stable: it would take 17 days for its spinning speed to decrease by 50 per cent, something that would typically happen more quickly due to interactions between the magnet and its environment. “In terms of how many turns it makes before slowing down significantly, this is in the same league as the Earth’s spinning,” he says. “This, so far, is the fastest magnetically levitated rotor.” The record for the fastest rotating human-made object is also held by a levitated sphere, but that one was nano-sized, so invisible to the naked eye, and levitated by laser beams.

Because the rotor experiences essentially no friction, and it is magnetic and cold, its behaviour is very sensitive to its environment, which makes it a promising sensor. The team has already successfully tested it as a gauge of vacuum at very low temperatures. Wang says this could be useful for builders of quantum computers, which often must be kept extremely cold and isolated in order to work.

Benjamin Stickler at Ulm University in Germany says the levitated spinning magnet could also be used to precisely sense and measure magnetic fields.

It could also be a promising platform for tests of fundamental physics, such as looking for effects related to dark matter particles, or sensing gravitational waves at so far unexplored frequencies, says team member Andrea Vinante at the National Research Council in Italy. Additionally, at very low temperatures quantum effects become dominant, so it could even be used for explorations of quantum mechanics and its interplay with gravity at micrometre scales, he says.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough involving a record-breaking fast-spinning magnet with potential applications in fundamental physics, quantum technology, and sensing. The impact is broad and meaningful for scientific progress and future technology development, with detailed context and implications provided.

articles.title: Preprint platform offers to pay researchers to review papers, but questions remain
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03442-zA reviewer can earn US$200 through XSci’s scheme if they deliver their work within five days.
articles.content:
Paying researchers to review papers is seen as a potential solution to clearing the peer-reviewing backlog.Credit: UpPiJ/iStock via Getty

A preprint platform is paying researchers for reviewing preprints uploaded by other scientists, reigniting debates about whether peer reviewers should be paid.

XSci, which launched in September, will reward a reviewer with US$200 if they send their feedback within five days of accepting the task and $100 if they do so between five and ten days. The fee is covered by other researchers, who pay XSci to have their preprints reviewed by scholars. The preprint website, which does not publish a journal, charges each author $399 for a round of review or $249 if they make their review report public.

The system enables authors to receive comments quickly while compensating reviewers for their time and effort, says Shumiao Ouyang, the founder of XSci, the start-up firm incorporated in Delaware that runs the platform. The company has received around $500,000 from private investors and is trying to raise more funds, Ouyang says.

A publishing platform that places code front and centre

“What authors get is an answer, usually within about five to ten days, to the question they care about most: does this paper have a real chance at the journals I am aiming at? Today, that answer can take months, and in some fields, years,” says Ouyang, who is an economist at the University of Oxford, UK. XSci also charges authors up to $19 to have their preprints reviewed by a range of artificial-intelligence programs, although access to some AI tools is free.

Several researchers interviewed by Nature say that XSci’s business model is interesting, but that its future will depend mostly on whether it can attract authors to use its human-reviewing service.

“Will authors be willing to pay such a fee? Where does the money come from?” asks developmental biologist and toxicologist Daniel Gorelick at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston, Texas, who has served as editor-in-chief of Biology Open since July 2023.

But Gorelick also says that cash payments are “a powerful incentive”. Biology Open, an open-access journal published by The Company of Biologists, has been paying reviewers £220 (or $280) per manuscript since 2024 through a programme called Fast and Fair. The payment is issued to the reviewer if they send in their work on time and if its quality meets the editors’ expectations.

Ouyang expects XSci’s core authors to be doctoral and postdoctoral students, as well as early-career researchers “who often cannot wait for a year or more for a journal’s decision”.

Pay-per-review

Peer reviewers are conventionally expected to review manuscripts as a service to the scientific community, rather than for a fee. By paying them at the preprint stage, Ouyang says, XSci intends to tackle challenges that dog the academic publishing industry today: how to convince scholars to review the work of others and to do it quickly.

Several studies1–3 have shown that journal editors are finding it increasingly difficult to source reviewers for various reasons, including a rising number of submissions and academics’ growing workloads. These and other issues often lead to a long review time, which can range from a few weeks to several months.

XSci states on its website that academics can register their interest to be paid reviewers. But in reality, says Ouyang, a scholar must be invited by the website to review a manuscript. The website nevertheless has a ‘register interest’ field for practical reasons because, he explains, “it tells us how many willing researchers there are in each field.”

Shumiao Ouyang is an economist at the University of Oxford, UK, and founder of XSci.Credit: Yizhen Zhang

Ouyang says that XSci has developed an AI program to help find suitable reviewers quickly. Once an author uploads their manuscript to XSci and chooses the human-reviewing option, the AI tool will compile a ranking of potential reviewers by screening candidates from three sources: the scientists who wrote the papers that the manuscript cites, those scholars’ regular collaborators and researchers who have published papers on similar topics in the author’s target journals. The AI program will rank, then e-mail, potential reviewers one by one. Each potential reviewer has 12 hours to accept the job, says Ouyang.

If the reviewer thinks that the manuscript could be published in the author’s target journals after reasonable changes, the preprint will be given a badge on the website, demonstrating that it has been reviewed and is endorsed by the reviewer.

In time, XSci hopes to form partnerships with journal publishers that would allow the journals’ editors to use XSci’s review reports as part of their assessments. This would happen only if the authors and reviewers both agree to the reports being shared, Ouyang says. The idea is that editors can decide what to do with XSci’s reviews: whether to use them to replace one round of their own reviews or as external references, he adds. In follow-up questions from Nature, however, Ouyang stressed that the badge would merely “become useful information for an editor”.

“Whether a journal gives them any weight is the entirely the journal’s decision,” he added.

Pros and cons

In 2025, Fast and Fair helped to slash the time that Biology Open editors spent making the first decision about a manuscript from an average of 37.7 working days under the free-reviewing route to an average of 5.5 working days, according to a preprint co-authored by Gorelick4. The programme also led to review invitations having a higher acceptance rate and a higher completion rate of accepted tasks, the study found.

But a separate study found that paying reviewers did not achieve substantial improvements. Editors at Critical Care Medicine, a journal published by Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, carried out a six-month experiment in which they sent reviewers invitations with or without monetary incentives in alternating two-week blocks5. They found that 50% of review invitations with a $250 cash reward resulted in a peer-review report in 14 days, compared with 42% of invitations without the fee. Paid reviewers also delivered their work just one day quicker on average than did non-paid reviewers.

“It didn’t move the needle too much,” says David Maslove, one of the editors who co-authored in the study and a clinician-scientist at Queen’s University in Kingston, Canada.

‘Getting paid to review is justice’: journal pays peer reviewers in cryptocurrency

A paying system comes with challenges, researchers warn. There need to be stringent quality controls, as well as policies in place to ensure that reviewers don’t game the system and publishers don’t take advantage of reviewers, Gorelick says. “You can’t just pay reviewers and walk away,” he notes.

“XSci currently does not check the quality of the reviews done by the reviewers before they are released to the authors,” says Jeffery Poon, publishing and editorial lead of XSci. If the authors are not satisfied with what they receive, they can initiate an appeal through XSci, Poon notes. XSci plans to provide tools to reviewers to help them check their own work, but the team is still working out how that could be implemented in reality, he adds.
